questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Gradient Vector Field of a Function
questions.problem: Find the gradient vector field of the function $f(x,y)=\operatorname{tan}⁡(x-2y).$
questions.worked_solution:
The gradient vector field of a function $f$ is given by $∇f.$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{tan}⁡(x-2y)) \\  & ={sec}^{2}⁡(x-2y) \\ {f}_{y}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{tan}⁡(x-2y)) \\  & =-2{sec}^{2}⁡(x-2y)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the gradient vector field of $f(x,y)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\  & ={sec}^{2}⁡(x-2y)\,i-2{sec}^{2}⁡(x-2y)\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Find the gradient vector field of the function $f(x,y)=\sqrt{2x-1}-\sqrt{4y+1}.$
questions.worked_solution:
The gradient vector field of a function $f$ is given by $∇f.$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\sqrt{2x-1}-\sqrt{4y+1}) \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2x-1}} \\ {f}_{y}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\sqrt{2x-1}-\sqrt{4y+1}) \\  & =-\frac{2}{\sqrt{4y+1}}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the gradient vector field of $f(x,y)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2x-1}}\,i-\frac{2}{\sqrt{4y+1}}\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Gradient Vector Field of a Function
questions.problem: Find the gradient vector field of the function $f(x,y,z)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(xz+2y).$
questions.worked_solution:
The gradient vector field of a function $f$ is given by $∇f.$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(xz+2y)) \\  & =z\operatorname{cos}⁡(xz+2y) \\ {f}_{y}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(xz+2y)) \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡(xz+2y) \\ {f}_{z}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(xz+2y)) \\  & =x\operatorname{cos}⁡(xz+2y)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the gradient vector field of $f(x,y,z)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\,j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\,k \\  & =z\operatorname{cos}⁡(xz+2y)\,i+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(xz+2y)\,j+x\operatorname{cos}⁡(xz+2y)\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Find the gradient vector field of the function $f(x,y,z)=x\operatorname{ln}⁡(z-2y).$
questions.worked_solution:
The gradient vector field of a function $f$ is given by $∇f.$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x\operatorname{ln}⁡(z-2y)) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(z-2y) \\ {f}_{y}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(x\operatorname{ln}⁡(z-2y)) \\  & =-\frac{2x}{z-2y} \\ {f}_{z}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(x\operatorname{ln}⁡(z-2y)) \\  & =\frac{x}{z-2y}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the gradient vector field of $f(x,y,z)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\,j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\,k \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(z-2y)\,i-\frac{2x}{z-2y}\,j+\frac{x}{z-2y}\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Which of the following diagrams represents the gradient vector field of the function $f(x,y)=2y-x?$
questions.worked_solution:
The gradient vector field of a function $f$ is given by $∇f.$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2y-x) \\  & =-1 \\ {f}_{y}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2y-x) \\  & =2\end{aligned}
$$

So, the gradient vector field of $f(x,y)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\  & =-i+2\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have to sketch the vector field at the points $(-2,2),$ $(2,2),$ and $(2,-2).$

To sketch the vector field at the given points, we substitute their coordinates into the expression for $∇f.$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(-2,2) & =-i+2\,j \\ ∇f(2,2) & =-i+2\,j \\ ∇f(2,-2) & =-i+2\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we draw the vectors starting at the corresponding points and obtain the following diagram:

questions.worked_solution:
The gradient vector field of a function $f$ is given by $∇f.$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x+{y}^{2}) \\  & =1 \\ {f}_{y}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(x+{y}^{2}) \\  & =2y\end{aligned}
$$

So, the gradient vector field of $f(x,y)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\,i+2y\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have to sketch the vector field at the points $(-4,1),$ $(1,1),$ and $(3,-1).$

To sketch the vector field at the given points, we substitute their coordinates into the expression for $∇f.$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(-4,1) & =i+2\cdot 1\,j=i+2\,j \\ ∇f(1,1) & =i+2\cdot 1\,j=i+2\,j \\ ∇f(3,-1) & =i+2\cdot (-1)\,j=i-2\,j\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Which of the following diagrams represents the gradient vector field of the function $f(x,y)=2\operatorname{arctan}⁡(xy)?$
questions.worked_solution:
The gradient vector field of a function $f$ is given by $∇f.$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2\operatorname{arctan}⁡(xy)) \\  & =\frac{2y}{{x}^{2}{y}^{2}+1} \\ {f}_{y}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2\operatorname{arctan}⁡(xy)) \\  & =\frac{2x}{{x}^{2}{y}^{2}+1}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the gradient vector field of $f(x,y)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{2y}{{x}^{2}{y}^{2}+1}\,i+\frac{2x}{{x}^{2}{y}^{2}+1}\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Next, we have to sketch the vector field at the points $(-1,1),$ $(0,-2),$ and $(2,0).$

To sketch the vector field at the given points, we substitute their coordinates into the expression for $∇f.$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(-1,1) & =\frac{2\cdot 1}{(-1)^{2}(1)^{2}+1}\,i+\frac{2\cdot (-1)}{(-1)^{2}(1)^{2}+1}\,j=i-j \\ ∇f(0,-2) & =\frac{2\cdot (-2)}{(0)^{2}(-2)^{2}+1}\,i+\frac{2\cdot 0}{(0)^{2}(-2)^{2}+1}\,j=-4\,i \\ ∇f(2,0) & =\frac{2\cdot 0}{(2)^{2}(0)^{2}+1}\,i+\frac{2\cdot 2}{(2)^{2}(0)^{2}+1}\,j=4\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we draw the vectors starting at the corresponding points and obtain the following diagram:

questions.problem: Which of the following diagrams represents the gradient vector field of the function $f(x,y)=\frac{{x}^{3}-2{y}^{2}}{4}?$
questions.worked_solution:
The gradient vector field of a function $f$ is given by $∇f.$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{{x}^{3}-2{y}^{2}}{4}) \\  & =\frac{3}{4}{x}^{2} \\ {f}_{y}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\frac{{x}^{3}-2{y}^{2}}{4}) \\  & =-y\end{aligned}
$$

So, the gradient vector field of $f(x,y)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{3}{4}{x}^{2}\,i-y\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have to sketch the vector field at the points $(-2,2),$ $(2,-3),$ and $(2,1).$

To sketch the vector field at the given points, we substitute their coordinates into the expression for $∇f.$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(-2,2) & =\frac{3}{4}\cdot (-2)^{2}\,i-2\,j=3\,i-2\,j \\ ∇f(2,-3) & =\frac{3}{4}\cdot {2}^{2}\,i-(-3)\,j=3\,i+3\,j \\ ∇f(2,1) & =\frac{3}{4}\cdot {2}^{2}\,i-\,j=3\,i-j\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we draw the vectors starting at the corresponding points and obtain the following diagram:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14044724/assets/26a5c0123d93231a800456e9f06f6ba7450861838c87d4d1b3ae77dab4cec6cf.png)

questions.problem: Which of the following diagrams represents the gradient vector field of the function $f(x,y)=\frac{(y-2x)^{2}}{2}?$
questions.worked_solution:
The gradient vector field of a function $f$ is given by $∇f.$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{(y-2x)^{2}}{2}) \\  & =-2(y-2x) \\ {f}_{y}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\frac{(y-2x)^{2}}{2}) \\  & =y-2x\end{aligned}
$$

So, the gradient vector field of $f(x,y)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\  & =-2(y-2x)\,i+(y-2x)\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have to sketch the vector field at the points $(1,1),$ $(1,3),$ and $(-2,-3).$

To sketch the vector field at the given points, we substitute their coordinates into the expression for $∇f.$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(1,1) & =-2\cdot (1-2\cdot 1)\,i+(1-2\cdot 1)\,j=2\,i-j \\ ∇f(1,3) & =-2\cdot (3-2\cdot 1)\,i+(3-2\cdot 1)\,j=-2\,i+j \\ ∇f(-2,-3) & =-2\cdot (-3-2\cdot (-2))\,i+(-3-2\cdot (-2))\,j=-2\,i+j\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we draw the vectors starting at the corresponding points and obtain the following diagram:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14044724/assets/2595c11a1b30fee9d76028010d2c7e608250c0d48ce0191d7da2a5412af6a110.png)

questions.problem: Which of the following could be the gradient vector field of the function $f(x,y)={x}^{2}-{y}^{2}?$
questions.worked_solution:
We start by plotting some level curves of the function:

- Setting $f(x,y)=-1,$ we get ${x}^{2}-{y}^{2}=-1,$ which gives the vertical hyperbola ${y}^{2}-{x}^{2}=1$

- Setting $f(x,y)=0,$ we get ${x}^{2}-{y}^{2}=0,$ which gives the pair of lines $y=\pm x$

- Setting $f(x,y)=2,$ we get ${x}^{2}-{y}^{2}=2,$ which gives the horizontal hyperbola $\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}-\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}=1$

- $⋯$

Continuing in this way, we get the following contour plot:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14044724/assets/cecc7f28c20523aac9f153022d64da4233ce995e05df3b3e2886b7fb3b20d089.png)

Note that $f(x,y)$ increases as we move from left to right in the right half-plane $x>0,$ and increases as we move from right-to-left in the left half-plane $x<0.$

Now, we recall the following facts:

- The gradient field vectors of a function $f(x,y)$ always lie perpendicular to its level curves.

- Moreover, the vectors point in the direction where $f(x,y)$ increases.

With this in mind, we can add the vector field to the contour plot, giving the following picture.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14044724/assets/037f46d3fdd190749c2aefe51222475fdd337a7b3ce53e6809048e3491a31a47.png)

So, the corresponding gradient field is as follows:

canonical_examples.problem: Find the gradient vector field of the function $f(x,y) = e^{2x-3y}.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The gradient vector field of a function $f$ is given by $\nabla f.$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({e}^{2x-3y}) \\  & =2{e}^{2x-3y} \\ {f}_{y}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({e}^{2x-3y}) \\  & =-3{e}^{2x-3y}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the gradient vector field of $f(x,y)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\  & =2{e}^{2x-3y}\,i-3{e}^{2x-3y}\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The gradient vector field of a function $f$ is given by $\nabla f.$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2{y}^{2}-{x}^{2}) \\  & =-2x \\ {f}_{y}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2{y}^{2}-{x}^{2}) \\  & =4y\end{aligned}
$$

So, the gradient vector field of $f(x,y)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\  & =-2x\,i+4y\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have to sketch the vector field at the points $(2,1),$ $(-2,1),$ and $(1,-1).$

To sketch the vector field at the given points, we substitute their coordinates into the expression for $\nabla f.$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(2,1) & =-2\cdot 2\,i+4\cdot 1\,j=-4\,i+4\,j \\ ∇f(-2,1) & =-2\cdot (-2)\,i+4\cdot 1\,j=4\,i+4\,j \\ ∇f(1,-1) & =-2\cdot 1\,i+4\cdot (-1)\,j=-2\,i-4\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we draw the vectors at their corresponding points and obtain the following diagram:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14044724/assets/b88c62b154cecaace206248b62f72b8aa1f71662c0427adfbbabd5c2b4738a6b.png)

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14044724/assets/c4d5f211c3bf3d306c6dc14205311c60eeaaf55de89f8af571ec0fa9e5add8a6.png)

 

Which of the above diagrams could be the gradient vector field of the function $f(x,y) = xy?$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We start by plotting some level curves of the function:

- Setting $f(x,y) = -1,$ we get $xy = -1,$ which gives the hyperbola $y=-\dfrac 1x$

- Setting $f(x,y) = 0,$ we get $xy = 0,$ that is, the lines $y=0$ and $x=0$

- Setting $f(x,y) = 1,$ we get $xy =1,$ that is, the hyperbola $y=\dfrac 1x$

- Setting $f(x,y) = -2,$ we get $xy =-2,$ that is, the hyperbola $y=-\dfrac 2x$

- $\cdots$

Continuing in this way, we get the following contour plot:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14044724/assets/f95c7ab30b7b02d67ceec039792e649a900dbece2896cc1e63341fcba9fc794f.png)

Note that $f(x,y)$ increases as we move from left to right in the upper half-plane $y > 0,$ and increases as we move from right-to-left in the lower half-plane $y < 0.$

Now, we recall the following facts:

- The gradient field vectors of a function $f(x,y)$ always lie perpendicular to its level curves.

- Moreover, the vectors point in the direction where $f(x,y)$ increases.

With this in mind, we can add the vector field to the contour plot, giving the following picture.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14044724/assets/3d6be27e083bb2e8b508cca31671e5cb4ea4e39b366a99f1dd194a5ea8ffcd3b.png)

So, the corresponding gradient field is as follows:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14044724/assets/996b5678396b4e9a91a4c55697442895331a7a6e4f8ec3eed550ea86845e44f4.png)

       

Therefore, the correct answer is III.
